I feel like an idiot warning you not to download a free game, but your time is more valuable than Spartan Survivors. I've played my share of low-effort Vampire Survivors clones, even the outright scam that is Artifact Seeker, and Spartan is by far the worst I've sampled of the genre. [h3] Reasons to Avoid [/h3] Basic "Survivors" staples are missing. 1. There's no breakdown at the end of the match showing how much damage each weapon did. Figuring out which weapon is the most efficient is pure guess work. 2. There are passive skills for increasing the number of projectiles, but not for increasing duration (unless one pops up [i] very [/i] late in the game). So picking projectile weapons gives you an immediate advantage. 3. Rounds only last five minutes at the most, which isn't enough time to fully upgrade your arsenal. Even playing on Legendary difficulty, I never maxed out more than two weapons. 4. The game is absurdly easy. I never died, or even came close to dying, at any time during my play through. The moment you can play on Legendary, do it. Even then, it will only increase the amount of time you spend in each round. The rounds are still pre-school simple. It's pretty common to clear a level on normal difficulty in two minutes. Two. 5. All characters are unlocked from the start. I almost finished the game (in two hours, yes) and never unlocked a single new character. I don't think I unlocked any passive skills either. All I got were increasingly powerful weapons that made an already easy game even easier. 6. Nothing interesting ever happens. This isn't like Vampire Survivors, where you're nuking the screen by the end of the round and the entire world is blanketed in enemies. You just keep wandering around, getting upgrades every two seconds. There's a difference between mindless and mind [i] numbing. [/i] 7. The levels are just square arenas. Nothing to explore, nothing to unlock, no gimmicks. There's zero difference between any of the levels. Why have different levels at all? The graphics are so minimal, you don't even get new objects to look at. The floor color changes. That's it. 8. There's no reason to pick any character besides "Bathrobe." He has a flamethrower from the start and a passive skill that dramatically increases his stats. Unless you unlock that skill for everyone at the very end of the game, it's unique to him. Balance? What's balance? 9. The enemies just walk into you. I know that's how most Survivors games work, but if you're going to go through the trouble of hijacking the Halo IP, at least make the enemies do what they do in Halo. Give the Jackals shields. Have enemies fire projectiles. Surround the Elites with an entourage of Grunts. Do [i] anything [/i] to change up the formula. 10. Weapons and passive skills don't work together to evolve the weapon. In fact, weapons don't evolve at all. It's not like Vampire Survivors, where pairing a certain weapon with a certain passive will cause the weapon to transform after it's been maxed out. This means one of the most basic elements that makes a Survivors game enjoyable is missing. There's no thought in your weapons selection. There's no strategy. You just pick whatever weapons appeal to your lizard brain and go for it. 11. Enemies don't even drop upgrade chests. You just level up, select the weapon you want to improve, and go about your day. So an essential element of RNG that makes the game unpredictable is nowhere to be found here. 12. The developer needs to take a grammar class. It's [i] number [/i] of projectiles, not amount. "Amount" is only used for abstract concepts that can't be quantified, like an amount of bravery or an amount of discipline. For anything that can theoretically be numbered, whether it be bullets, stars, or newborn kittens, use "number." And the plural of "knife" is "knives." Obvious mistakes like that make your game look unprofessional. Have some pride in what you create. Yeah, the game is free, but you only have so much time on this earth. Don't spend it with Spartan Survivors. Just pay three dollars and get a real Survivors game.

Rating: 9/10 (Overall Game) | 0/10 (Canonical Fidelity of Level 1) Hours Played: 489.7 hours (Dedicated to analyzing Level 1’s lore only, strictly the itch version) Tags: Deep Lore, Pedantic, Needs an Errata, Highly Recommended (with caveats) Let me be unequivocally clear at the outset: Spartan Survivors is, in terms of pure gameplay loop, a phenomenal contribution to the twin-stick bullet-hell/roguelite-lite genre. The feel of the Assault Rifle, the explosive satisfaction of the Plasma Grenades—it’s all there. The team has captured the visceral kineticism of the Halo sandbox perfectly. However, we are not here to discuss the elegance of the upgrade path or the satisfying damage numbers. We are here to discuss a canonical transgression so egregious, so utterly contradictory to the sacrosanct textual foundation established by the venerable, legendary, and highly acclaimed author Eric Nylund, that it threatens to collapse the entire scaffolding of the original conflict. I speak, of course, of the very first level: The Pillar of Autumn. The Blasphemy of Level One: Huragok in the Holodeck The level, "The Pillar of Autumn," aims to recreate the frantic, last-ditch defense and subsequent escape of the UNSC cruiser following the cataclysmic fall of Reach. We are dropped onto the smoking, sparking decks, fighting through waves of frantic Covenant forces—Elites, Grunts. All good, all accurate to the historical events documented in Halo: Combat Evolved and elaborated upon with exquisite detail in William C Dietz' Halo: The Flood. And then... you see them. The unmistakable, gently floating, tentacled, and utterly out-of-place silhouettes of the Huragok—the Engineers. I must insist: This is not merely an inaccuracy; it is apocryphal. Why This Breaks the Lore (A Dissertation): The presence of the delicate, biologically engineered Forerunner construction units known as the Huragok on the Pillar of Autumn during this initial, desperate engagement is an absolute impossibility within the timeline. First Contact and Discovery: The greater bulk of the UNSC personnel, especially those involved in the events of the Fall of Reach and the initial discovery of Installation 04, were utterly unaware of the existence of the Engineers. Their true nature and frequent use by the Covenant as living tools only became a widespread, recognized factor later in the Human-Covenant War, specifically involving events detailed in later novels (such as the actions leading up to the Battle of Earth and the Ark). The Pillar of Autumn Manifest: The Covenant forces attacking the Autumn were a purely combat-focused pursuit fleet. Their objective was to neutralize the ship and retrieve the AI construct, Cortana. They were not undertaking deep, technical salvage operations or major infrastructural repairs on a small, retreating flagship like the Truth and Reconciliation—a ship which, in itself, only appears much later in the ring structure. Introducing a non-combatant, highly sensitive support organism into the initial boarding action on a ship about to crash-land is tactically absurd and canonically unfounded. The Textual Evidence (Nylund’s Authority): Eric Nylund, whose works provide the deepest character and historical context for this period, focuses rigorously on the established Covenant hierarchy of combatants. As well as William C Dietz' Halo: The Flood is a moment-by-moment expansion of the initial game’s events. There are no asides, no hushed mentions, and no environmental evidence of Huragok involvement in the defense of the Autumn's bridge or the subsequent escape pod deployments. To retroactively inject the Engineers here is to fundamentally rewrite the dramatic tension and the known composition of the enemy forces at that pivotal, world-changing moment. Their absence is a feature, not a bug, of the original narrative. Conclusion: To the developers, I say this: You have built a mechanically excellent game. But the integrity of the fictional universe must be maintained. Every time I see a shimmering Huragok floating near the blast doors of the Autumn, entering through a hull breach it canonically should not be near, a piece of my soul shrivels. I recommend Spartan Survivors highly, but only if you are willing to mentally retcon Level 1. Please, for the sake of the canonical purity established by the legendary author Eric Nylund. Until then, I must dock three points from the Level 1 score for this egregious lore lapse. May your future updates respect the sacred texts.

Despite this, I will still be maintaining the stance of the original review as this decision has caused very visible performance issues with the game, inconsistencies and obviously the focused "Please refresh this page" crash. A very shallow Survivorslike, very few items so every run feels the same. The weapons do feel distinct, minus maybe the grenades, but the mid-run upgrades are just super noninteresting. All they are are boring stat ups, or actively detrimental to the run if you're looking for extra challenge or playing with random choice enabled. There are no synergies in the game whatsoever except for a perk that makes explosives bigger and the +1 projectile upgrade just being better on weapons that shoot fewer projectiles. But there is such a small pool that you can get these upgrades every single run by just looking for them. Half the cast of characters are also both super nothing, and also I have no idea who they are. This game feels very neck-deep in Halo community references that I am just unaware of. I've played like 10 Halo games but I know nothing of it's content creators or games past Spartan Strike, but thats on me. This game also just, runs terribly for me, like 10 fps terrible. It spawns too many enemies it can keep up with. Enemy variance isnt great either, they all mostly do the same thing, just again, different stats, or maybe they have a gun. This is probably the game's least weak weakness though if that makes sense. Like i feel like i should mention it but its more of a nitpick compared to my other issues. If you want to play a good free Survivorslike/Bullet Heaven, try out Holocure, just mind the anime aesthetics. Honestly you could just look up "good free survivorlikes[/bulletheavens]" and get way better games that are a better use of your time, and have way more in the package to play with. OH ALSO ONE MORE THING. MAKE SURE YOU GO BACK TO THE MAIN MENU AFTER LEVELING UP A FEW TIMES AND PRESS THE "UPGRADE" TAB TO GAIN METAPROGRESSION UPGRADES. I DIDNT REALIZE THIS WAS A FEATURE UNTIL THE END OF THE GAME.

I’ve played Spartan Survivors for about 2 hours, and I want to start by saying: this is actually a game I can recommend—especially since it’s free. But then why am I giving it a negative review? The game clearly takes inspiration from Vampire Survivors, which is both a strength and a weakness. On one hand, the gameplay feels familiar and works fine—combat feels decent, weapons are okay, and the enemies do their job. It’s easy to jump into and play right away. On the other hand, it also feels very simple and a bit too “basic.” The graphics are fine, but the map feels generic and doesn’t really offer anything interesting to explore. The biggest issue for me is the lack of information and polish. You can choose different characters, but the game doesn’t tell you what weapons or abilities they have. That means you have to start a run just to find out, which feels unnecessarily frustrating. It also feels like the developers haven’t fully implemented the systems that make roguelite games really shine. Right now, it comes across more like an early version or a test build, where the foundation is there, but many important details are still missing. That being said, you can feel the potential. It seems like a project where the developers genuinely want to make a good game and might be listening to feedback. So yes—give it a try, especially since it’s free. But in its current state, it’s just not strong enough yet. Score: 5/10 Not bad, but not good either—for now. I’m looking forward to future updates.

Spartan Survivors won’t win any award for its simplicistic artstyle and quite basic bullet heaven formula. Yet, for a free Halo fan game, I have a hard time asking for much more. The gameplay loop is enjoyable. The game is packed with Halo-themed characters, weapons, enemies and locations. There’s 10 levels and much to unlock. It’s currently only playable on PC, but it’ll hit Xbox consoles in the future, as well. Whether now or when it hits consoles, do give this one a fair shot if you’re into Halo, as it’s clearly a project made with passion by someone who loves the IP.
